description: We’re Orbitalists, a team of 8th graders who build with code and a passion for space. Fluent in C++ and Python, we created an educational game that makes orbital mechanics intuitive and fun, turning complex physics into something anyone can explore and play. Despite being among the youngest participants, we’ve competed against older age groups and held our own. Curiosity, teamwork, and determination are what carry us into orbit.
summary: Welcome to ORBITALIS! For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we didn’t just build a game, we built a flight simulator for the laws of the universe. Meet your spacecraft: small, silent, and completely in your hands. There is no autopilot here. You decide how fast to go, when to burn, and where to aim, and gravity answers every decision instantly. Burn forward to climb higher and you’ll discover something wild: you end up moving slower. Miss your timing and watch your orbit stretch into a long ellipse. Get it right and you’ll feel what mission designers feel when a trajectory finally clicks. This isn’t a lecture, it’s you in the pilot’s seat, learning Newton’s gravitation, Kepler’s laws, orbital velocity and delta-v by flying them, failing and flying again. Under the hood, the Godot Engine keeps the experience light and fast, while the JR Orrery plugin drives accurate Keplerian orbits and spacecraft trajectories at real astronomical scales. This is orbital mechanics like you’ve never seen it: not in formulas or textbook diagrams, but in the palm of your hand, as a playful, high-stakes mission.
details:
ORBITALIS: Fly the Physics

The idea

Every satellite, space station and planet obeys the same quiet rule: gravity pulls, speed resists, and the balance between the two draws an orbit. Most people meet that rule as an equation on a whiteboard, and it never becomes real. ORBITALIS was built to change that. It puts a spacecraft in the player’s hands and lets them find out for themselves how motion in space actually works, one decision at a time.

A session in ORBITALIS

The player launches a spacecraft and takes control of its velocity in real time. A small change in speed is not a number on a quiz, it is a visible bend in the path. Push a little harder and the orbit stretches into an ellipse. Slow down and the craft drops toward the planet. Burn forward to climb higher and something surprising happens: the spacecraft ends up moving slower at the higher altitude. Most players expect the opposite, and that moment of surprise is where the learning happens. Because time can be accelerated, a long orbit plays out in seconds, so a player can try an idea, see the result and try again within a minute. Nothing is lost by failing. A bad burn simply shows the player exactly what the physics does, and the next attempt is better for it.

What players take away

ORBITALIS is built around a small set of ideas that unlock most of spaceflight. Players meet Newton’s Law of Universal Gravitation as the force that shapes every path. They see Kepler’s Laws of Planetary Motion in action as orbits become ellipses, speed changes along the path, and size sets the period. They build a feel for orbital velocity, the one right speed for a given altitude. And they begin to think in delta-v (Δv), the budget of speed change that real mission designers spend to move from one trajectory to another. The goal is not memorized formulas, but intuition: after a few minutes, a player should be able to predict what a burn will do before they make it.

Who it is for

ORBITALIS is for students who find orbital mechanics abstract, for teachers who want a hands-on demonstration that does not need a lab, and for anyone who has looked at a launch and wondered how it works. It assumes no physics background, and it rewards curiosity more than prior knowledge. Since it is built entirely on free, open-source tools, it runs on ordinary computers and is easy to share.

Under the hood

ORBITALIS is built with the Godot Engine, a free, open-source, MIT-licensed platform for 2D and 3D. We chose it because it is lightweight, fast to iterate on and well suited to a project with a short timeline. Its node-based architecture keeps the scene, spacecraft, interface and orbital bodies organized, and GDScript, its readable scripting language, handles our gameplay logic.

The orbital motion is powered by the JR Orrery plugin for Godot 4.7+, a toolkit for building solar systems, planetary orbits, spacecraft trajectories and orbital maps in 2D, 3D or both. It drives analytical Keplerian orbits and GPU ballistic trajectories, so the behavior on screen follows real orbital rules rather than hand-tuned animation. Its physics scale is separate from its visual scale, which lets us show realistic astronomical distances in a way a player can read. It tracks each orbit relative to its local parent body, which avoids the floating-point jitter that can ruin large-scale simulations, and it hands off automatically between gravity wells as a spacecraft moves between them. Building on this plugin let us spend our time on the learning experience rather than on writing a physics solver.

What makes ORBITALIS creative

The physics is not a skin over the game, it is the game. Every orbit the player sees is a genuine consequence of the rules, so playing well and understanding the science are the same activity. We replaced charts and equations with cause and effect, and we designed the experience so that the most valuable thing a player can do is try something that might not work.

What we considered

We weighed accuracy against clarity, aiming for a simulation that behaves realistically and still reads at a glance. We designed for beginners, so controls are simple and feedback is immediate. We chose open tools so the project stays free and open to improvement. And because of our time limit, we focused on a few core ideas and made sure each one is something a player can actually experience, rather than trying to cover all of spaceflight. ORBITALIS is a learning tool, not a full mission-planning suite, and it does not attempt to model every real-world effect.

Where it could go next

The same foundation could support more missions, additional planets and moons, and richer challenges such as planning transfers between orbits. It could also grow into a classroom resource with guided lessons for teachers.
